_meta.status: RESEARCH OUTPUT — PART (RICE, TOMATO, POTATO). NOT merged into shared/i18n. Requires human review and Hindi authoring.

rules.faithfulRendering: Every English string says what a source fetched on 2026-08-13 says, in plain words. Nothing was added — no treatment, threshold, weather condition or plant part that a source did not publish. The source wording behind each key is in the matching entry's `publishedSymptoms` and `sourceRefs[].note` in crops.diseases.part-rtp.json.
rules.noDosages: docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3. No pesticide product name, active ingredient, concentration, spray rate or fertiliser dose appears in any string here, even where the cited source publishes them. Diseases whose sources recommend chemical control carry a nextStep string routing the farmer to KVK / Kisan Call Centre 1800-180-1551 instead.
rules.hindiIsNull: Every value in `hi` is null. No Hindi-language official source was fetched in this pass, and CLAUDE.md rule 8 forbids unsourced agronomic translation. The `hi` block lists every key so a Hindi-literate reviewer has an explicit worklist rather than an empty object. See gap D1.
rules.unitsAsPrinted: Where a source prints a measurement it is reproduced in the source's own unit. The UF/IFAS target-spot temperature band (°F) was NOT converted and is therefore not surfaced at all.

en.disease.RICE_BLAST.symptom.1: Small bluish-green flecks appear on the leaves.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.symptom.2: The flecks grow into spindle-shaped spots with a grey or ashy centre and a dark brown margin.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.symptom.3: Black lesions form on the nodes and girdle them. Affected nodes may break, and everything above the infected node dies.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.symptom.4: Lesions on the neck of the panicle are greyish brown. The neck is girdled and the panicle falls over.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.symptom.5: In a severe attack the whole crop looks blasted or burnt.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.inspect.1: Look at the leaves for spindle-shaped spots with a grey centre and a dark brown edge.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.inspect.2: Check the nodes and the neck of the panicle for black or greyish-brown girdling lesions, and see whether any panicles have fallen over.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.inspect.3: The published action thresholds are 3 to 5 lesions per leaf for leaf blast, and 2 to 5 neck-infected plants per square metre for neck blast.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.nextStep.1: Remove weed hosts from the bunds.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.nextStep.2: Do not apply extra nitrogen. Published guidance is to split the nitrogen into three applications.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.prevention.1: Plant a variety resistant to blast. The published guidance calls this the most practical and economical way to control the disease.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.prevention.2: Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser. High nitrogen favours the disease.
en.disease.RICE_BLAST.prevention.3: Sow disease-free and insect-free pure seed.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.symptom.1: Minute brown dots appear on the coleoptile, leaf blade, leaf sheath and glume.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.symptom.2: The dots become cylindrical or oval, dark brown with a yellow halo. Spots measure about 0.5 to 2.0 mm across and join into larger patches.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.symptom.3: The leaf dries up. A badly affected nursery can be recognised from a distance by its scorched appearance, and seedlings die.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.symptom.4: Dark brown or black spots also appear on the glumes, discolouring the grain and reducing grain quality and weight.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.inspect.1: Look on the leaves for oval, dark brown spots with a yellow halo.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.inspect.2: Check the glumes on the panicle for dark brown or black spots.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.inspect.3: The published action threshold is 2 to 3 spots per leaf together with 2 to 3 infected plants per square metre.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.nextStep.1: Do not apply extra nitrogen. The published guidance states that excess nitrogen aggravates this disease.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.nextStep.2: Published guidance also lists chemical control and seed treatment for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.prevention.1: Grow a resistant variety. The published guidance describes this as the most economical means of control.
en.disease.RICE_BROWN_SPOT.prevention.3: Where the soil is known to be low in plant-available silicon, the published guidance recommends amending it with calcium silicate slag.
en.disease.RICE_BACTERIAL_LEAF_BLIGHT.sympt: Water-soaked, translucent lesions appear near the leaf margin.
The lesions grow in length and width with a wavy margin and turn straw yellow.
Leaves show wavy yellowish-white or golden-yellow dying along the margin and dry back from the tip, curling, while the midrib stays intact.
Milky or opaque dewdrop-like beads of bacteria form on young lesions.
In the kresek phase, seen 1 to 3 weeks after transplanting, seedlings wilt and roll, turn greyish green to yellow, and the plant collapses.
en.disease.RICE_BACTERIAL_LEAF_BLIGHT.inspe: Look along the leaf margins for wavy, straw-yellow lesions that dry back from the leaf tip.
Look in the early morning for milky or opaque bacterial ooze on young lesions.
The published action thresholds are 2 to 3 infected leaves per square metre for leaf blight, and 2 to 3 affected plants per square metre for the kresek phase.
en.disease.RICE_BACTERIAL_LEAF_BLIGHT.nextS: Drain the field, except at the flowering stage of the crop.
Use balanced fertilisation and avoid excess nitrogen, especially late top dressing.
Remove weeds from the field and the bunds. Weeds are listed as a source of the bacteria.

Published guidance also lists chemical and antibiotic control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.RICE_BACTERIAL_LEAF_BLIGHT.preve: Raise the nursery in isolated upland conditions where possible.
Do not clip the tips of the seedlings at transplanting. Clipping is listed as a condition that favours the disease.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.symptom.1: Affected plants are stunted and produce fewer tillers.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.symptom.2: Leaves turn yellow or orange-yellow and may carry rust-coloured spots.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.symptom.3: Yellowing starts at the tip of the leaf and may extend down towards the lower part.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.symptom.4: Young leaves are often mottled with pale green to whitish stripes between the veins.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.symptom.5: Flowering is delayed. Panicles are small, do not emerge fully, and are mostly sterile or only partly filled.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.inspect.1: Compare the affected plants with their neighbours: look for shorter plants with fewer tillers.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.inspect.2: Look for green leafhoppers on the plants. The green leafhopper is the insect that carries this virus from plant to plant.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.inspect.3: The published action threshold is 1 tungro-infected plant per square metre together with 2 green leafhoppers per hill.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.nextStep.1: Set up light traps to attract the leafhopper vectors and to monitor how many there are.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists insecticide sprays against the leafhopper vector. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.prevention.2: Adjust the planting date and keep a fallow period.
en.disease.RICE_TUNGRO.prevention.3: Rotate the field with pulses or oilseeds.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.inspect.1: Walk the field and observe it weekly, in the morning, preferably before 9 a.m.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.inspect.2: Look at the soil, the water, the plants, the pests, the natural enemies and the weather together, and decide what to do from what the field is showing you.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.inspect.3: The published action thresholds for the common rice diseases are: leaf blast 3 to 5 lesions per leaf; brown spot 2 to 3 spots per leaf with 2 to 3 infected plants per square metre; bacterial leaf blight 2 to 3 infected leaves per square metre; tungro 1 infected plant per square metre.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.1: Select a suitable resistant or moderately resistant variety.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.2: Use disease-free and insect-free pure seed, and raise a healthy nursery.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.3: Plant on time and keep normal spacing of about 30 to 36 hills per square metre, depending on the duration of the variety.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.4: Use balanced fertiliser and micronutrients as per local recommendations.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.5: Destroy the leftover nursery, remove weeds from the field and clean the bunds.
en.disease.RICE_NORMAL.prevention.6: After harvest, flood the field thoroughly and plough it, to destroy the pests that survive in the stubble.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.1: Small black lesions appear first, mostly on the older, lower leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.2: The spots enlarge and show brown concentric rings in a bull's-eye pattern in the centre of the diseased area.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.3: The tissue around the spots may turn yellow. If high temperature and humidity follow, much of the foliage is killed.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.4: Lesions on the stems look like those on the leaves, and can girdle the plant if they occur near the soil line.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.5: The fruit is infected through the calyx or the stem attachment and carries brown concentric rings.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.1: Start with the older, lower leaves. This is where the first lesions appear.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.2: Look for concentric rings in the centre of the spot. This bull's-eye pattern is the identifying feature.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.3: Check the calyx end of the fruit, and the stem near the soil line.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.nextStep.1: Practise field sanitation and destroy infected plant debris. The fungus survives in debris in or on the soil for at least a year, and can also be carried on seed.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.nextStep.2: Destroy alternate host plants, and give light irrigation.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.2: Select healthy seeds and healthy seedlings.
en.disease.TOMATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.4: Do not apply too much nitrogen fertiliser. If the nitrogen dose is too high the crop becomes too succulent and more susceptible to insects and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.1: Water-soaked black lesions appear on the leaves and the stems.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.2: The lesions expand rapidly and the whole leaf dies.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.3: White fungal growth appears on the leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.4: Dark brown lesions form on the fruit, followed by soft rot and breakdown of the fruit.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.1: Look for lesions that are spreading quickly. This disease moves fast in cool nights, warm days and long wet spells from rain or fog.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.2: Look for white fungal growth on the affected leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.3: Check the fruit for dark brown lesions and soft rot.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.1: Practise field sanitation and destroy affected plants and debris.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.2: Destroy alternate host plants, and give light irrigation.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.2: Select healthy seeds and healthy seedlings, and follow proper spacing.
en.disease.TOMATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.3: Do not apply too much nitrogen fertiliser. If the nitrogen dose is too high the crop becomes too succulent and more susceptible to insects and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_SEPTORIA_LEAF_SPOT.sympto: Small, round to irregular spots with a grey centre and a dark margin appear on the leaves.
The spots usually start on the lower leaves and gradually advance upwards.
Spots join together, the leaves are blighted, and affected leaves can be shed completely.
Stems and flowers are sometimes attacked. Fruits are rarely attacked.
Less vigorous plants are usually the ones affected.
en.disease.TOMATO_SEPTORIA_LEAF_SPOT.inspec: Start with the lower leaves and work upwards.
Look for a grey centre with a dark margin. This distinguishes these spots from the ringed spots of early blight.
Note whether the affected plants are weak. Poor plant vigour from inadequate nutrition is listed as a condition that favours this disease.
en.disease.TOMATO_SEPTORIA_LEAF_SPOT.nextSt: Practise field sanitation and remove infected plant debris and solanaceous weeds, where the fungus survives between crops.
Pickers can carry this fungus on their hands and clothing. Handle affected plants last, and wash hands and clothes afterwards.

Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_SEPTORIA_LEAF_SPOT.preven: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases, and use healthy seeds and seedlings.
Keep the crop vigorous with nutrient management based on a soil test. Weak plants are the ones this disease attacks.
Follow proper spacing and rotate the crop.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.1: Small, brown, water-soaked, circular spots with a yellow halo appear on the leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.2: On older plants the infection is mostly on the older leaves, and can cause serious leaf fall.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.3: Small, water-soaked spots appear on green fruit. Ripe fruit is not susceptible.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.4: The centres of the fruit spots become irregular and light brown, with a sunken, rough, scabby surface.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.1: Start with the older, lower leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.2: Check the green fruit for small water-soaked spots that later become sunken and scabby.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.3: Note the recent weather. Outbreaks are usually traced back to heavy rainstorms in the area.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.1: Practise field sanitation. Remove infected plant debris, volunteer tomato plants and solanaceous weeds, where the bacteria survive.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.2: Do not save seed from an affected crop. The bacteria contaminate the seed surface and survive there.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_BACTERIAL_SPOT.prevention: Select healthy seeds and healthy seedlings, and a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.sy: The leaves roll downwards and become crinkled.
The newly emerging leaves show slight yellow colouring and later curl as well.
Older leaves become leathery and brittle.
The internodes are shortened and the plant produces many lateral branches, giving it a bushy look.
en.disease.TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.in: Turn the leaves over and look for whiteflies. The whitefly is the insect that carries this virus from plant to plant.
Check the newest leaves for yellow colouring and curling.
Compare plant height and shape with healthy neighbours: look for short internodes, many side branches and a bushy plant.
en.disease.TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.ne: Practise field sanitation. Remove and destroy affected plants, and remove alternate weed hosts.
Put up yellow sticky traps or cards, about 10 per acre, to reduce the whitefly population.

Published guidance also lists insecticides against the whitefly vector. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_YELLOW_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.pr: Raise the nursery under a net with a mesh fine enough to keep whiteflies out.
Take seed only from disease-free, healthy plants.
Remove and destroy infected plants in the nursery. Never transplant a seedling that already shows virus symptoms.
Raise a barrier crop of cereals such as maize, sorghum or bajra around the field.
Remove alternate weed hosts from and around the field.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.symptom.1: The leaves show light and dark green mottling.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.symptom.2: Young leaves often wilt on sunny days when the plant is first infected.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.symptom.3: The leaflets are distorted, puckered and smaller than normal, and are sometimes so indented that the leaf looks like a fern.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.symptom.4: The affected plant looks stunted, pale green and spindly.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.inspect.1: Look for a patchwork of light and dark green on the leaf, rather than spots with a definite edge.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.inspect.2: Check the shape of the leaflets: look for puckering, distortion and small, narrow, fern-like leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.nextStep.1: This virus spreads by touch. It travels on clothes, on the hands of working labour, on implements and in plant debris. Handle affected plants last, and wash hands and implements before touching healthy plants.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.nextStep.2: Remove and destroy the infected plants.
en.disease.TOMATO_MOSAIC_VIRUS.prevention.3: Select healthy seedlings and a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.symptom.1: The affected leaves turn reddish brown and bronzy.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.symptom.2: In a severe infestation there is fine silken webbing on the leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.symptom.4: Flower and fruit formation is affected.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.inspect.1: Turn the leaves over. Mites sit on the underside of the leaf. The adult mite is small and red.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.inspect.2: Pick five spots at random in the field, five plants at each spot, and count the young and adult mites on five leaves per plant.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.nextStep.1: Conserve the natural enemies that eat mites: predatory mites, rove beetles, ladybird beetles, lacewings, predatory thrips, anthocorid bugs, mirid bugs and predatory flies.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.nextStep.2: Published guidance also lists chemical control for mites. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests, and healthy seeds and seedlings.
en.disease.TOMATO_SPIDER_MITES.prevention.2: Follow proper spacing and proper irrigation.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.symptom.1: Pale or light green spots appear on the upper surface of the leaf, and later turn yellow or brown.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.symptom.2: On the underside of the leaf, opposite those spots, an olive-green velvety mould growth develops.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.symptom.3: The older, lower leaves are affected first and more severely, and the disease then moves upwards.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.symptom.4: Affected leaf tissue dies and the plant loses leaves.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.inspect.1: Turn the leaf over. The olive-green velvety growth on the underside, directly behind a pale spot on top, is the identifying feature of this disease.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.inspect.2: Start with the older, lower leaves, and check the humidity where the crop is growing. The spores germinate when relative humidity is above 85 per cent.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.nextStep.1: No Indian published guidance for this disease was found for this app, so no treatment is given here. Contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases, and healthy seeds and seedlings.
en.disease.TOMATO_LEAF_MOLD.prevention.2: Follow proper spacing and proper irrigation.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.symptom.1: Leaf lesions start as pinpoint dark brown spots.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.symptom.2: The centres become light brown to grey, with dark outer concentric rings, and are sometimes surrounded by yellowing.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.symptom.3: The lesions can join up quickly, blighting the leaf and causing early leaf fall. On leaf stalks and stems the lesions are dark brown and oval.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.symptom.4: On the fruit, damage starts as small, brown, sunken flecks that grow into deeply pitted lesions, and severely affected fruit can crack in an X or star shape as it ripens.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.inspect.1: Look for the concentric rings. Mature leaves are affected more than young leaves, and the disease spreads fastest inside a dense canopy where the leaves stay wet.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.inspect.2: Check the fruit for small sunken brown flecks and for star-shaped cracking.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.nextStep.1: No Indian published guidance for this disease was found for this app, so no treatment is given here. Contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases, and healthy seeds and seedlings.
en.disease.TOMATO_TARGET_SPOT.prevention.2: Follow proper spacing and proper irrigation.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.inspect.1: Start observing the field as soon as the crop is established after transplanting, and then every week.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.inspect.2: Pick five spots at random in the field and five plants at each spot, so that a problem showing up in patches is not missed.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.inspect.3: Turn the leaves over. Mites and whiteflies sit on the underside of the leaf, where they are easy to miss.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.prevention.2: Select healthy seeds and healthy seedlings.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.prevention.4: Improve soil health with mulching and green manuring.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.prevention.5: Manage nutrients from a soil test. If the nitrogen dose is too high the crop becomes too succulent and more susceptible to insects and diseases; if it is too low, growth is held back.
en.disease.TOMATO_HEALTHY.prevention.6: Irrigate properly and rotate the crop.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.1: Water-soaked spots appear on the leaves, grow larger, turn purple-brown and finally black.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.2: Affected leaves look blistered, as if scalded with hot water, and then rot and dry out.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.3: White growth develops on the under surface of the leaves. While the infection is active the underside looks as if it has been dusted with flour.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.4: The leaf stalks and stems are affected, often at the nodes. The stem breaks there and the plant topples over.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.5: Affected tubers show purplish-brown spots on the skin and a rusty-brown rot spreading from the surface towards the centre.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.symptom.6: This disease acts very quickly. If it is not controlled, infected plants can die within two or three days.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.1: Turn the leaves over and look for white, flour-like growth on the underside, behind the water-soaked spots.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.2: Check the stems at the nodes for blackening, and cut open a suspect tuber to look for rusty-brown rot spreading in from the skin.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.inspect.3: Watch the crop closely after cloudy, rainy days when humidity is above 90 per cent and night temperature is around 10 °C. These are the conditions in which this disease spreads.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.1: Act at once. This disease can kill infected plants within two or three days.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.2: Remove and destroy affected plant material. The pathogen survives in plant debris in the soil, and spreads through the soil and through infected seed tubers.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.nextStep.3: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551 straight away.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.2: Select healthy seed tubers. Diseased tubers are the main way this disease carries over from one crop to the next.
en.disease.POTATO_LATE_BLIGHT.prevention.3: Follow proper spacing and irrigate properly.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.1: Small black lesions appear first, mostly on the older, lower leaves.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.2: The spots are brown to black and necrotic, angular to oval, and marked with concentric rings in a bull's-eye pattern.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.3: Several spots join up and spread over the whole leaf, and the tissue around the spots may turn yellow.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.4: Lesions on the stems look like those on the leaves, and can girdle the plant if they occur near the soil line.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.symptom.5: The disease occurs both in the hills and in the plains.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.1: Start with the older, lower leaves.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.2: Look for the concentric rings in the centre of the spot. This bull's-eye pattern is the identifying feature.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.inspect.3: Watch the crop from the tuber-bulking stage onwards. Symptoms normally become obvious then and go on developing up to harvest.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.nextStep.1: Remove and destroy affected plant debris. The spores and fungal threads survive in the soil and in debris for more than 17 months.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.nextStep.2: Published guidance also lists chemical control for this disease. This app does not give pesticide doses. For a dose, contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests and diseases, and healthy seed tubers.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.2: Keep the crop vigorous with adequate manuring. Poor crop vigour and inadequate manuring are listed as conditions that favour this disease.
en.disease.POTATO_EARLY_BLIGHT.prevention.3: Follow proper spacing and irrigate properly.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.inspect.1: Monitor the field at least once a week: the soil, the water, the plants, the pests, the natural enemies and the weather.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.inspect.2: Decide what to do from what the field is showing you, and from the balance between pests and their natural enemies. Take direct action when it is needed, such as removing infested plants.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.prevention.1: Select a variety resistant or tolerant to the major pests.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.prevention.2: Select healthy seed tubers and healthy planting material.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.prevention.4: Improve soil health with mulching and green manuring where it applies.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.prevention.5: Manage nutrients from a soil test. If the nitrogen dose is too high the crop becomes too succulent and more susceptible to insects and diseases; if it is too low, growth is held back.
en.disease.POTATO_HEALTHY.prevention.6: Irrigate properly and rotate the crop.
